question: Company reports 200cr exceptional income from selling land. Analyst should:
before: Exceptional items are one-time, non-recurring. Strip out for sustainable earning power assessment. Adding to revenue or EBITDA overstates operational performance.
after:
Concept: Exceptional items are one-time, non-recurring gains or losses that do not reflect the company's underlying operational capacity. When assessing normalised or sustainable earnings, these items must be excluded to show what the business earns from its core activities.

Why this is correct: Exceptional income of ₹200 crore from a land sale is a capital event, not an operating result. Stripping it out reveals the company's true recurring earning power, which is what equity analysts use to project future cash flows and value the business.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Add to revenue — Revenue measures sales from ongoing business operations. A one-time land sale is not revenue and inflates the top line artificially, misleading anyone projecting future growth.

B) Include in EBITDA — EBITDA measures earnings from core operations before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Adding exceptional income overstates operational profitability and distorts comparability with peers and historical periods.

D) Ignore income statement entirely — The item must still be identified and disclosed on the income statement. The correct practice is to recognise it but exclude it from normalised earnings calculations, not to pretend it does not exist.

Intuition: Normalised earnings isolate operational performance from one-off events. In equity research, this is the foundation of earnings-power valuation models; mixing in exceptional items creates phantom earnings that will not repeat, leading to overvaluation and flawed investment decisions.
